title: Berggasse and Beyond: the Making and Unmaking of the Interior World
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Moravia to Vienna: the Making of a Mind

stops.name: Freiberg (Příbor), Moravia: the wool merchant's house
stops.campa: In a rented room on the Schlossergasse, above a locksmith's shop in the small Moravian town of Freiberg, Amalia Freud bears her first son to the wool merchant Jakob Freud, twenty years her senior. They name him Sigismund Schlomo. Jakob already has two grown sons from an earlier marriage; the infant's nephew John, older than his uncle, will be his first playmate and rival. The caul he is born in is kept by his mother as a talisman of destined greatness, the first of many signs she reads into her golden-haired boy.
suggested_refs: The birth house on Freud-Straße (Zámečnická) 117, Příbor, now the Sigmund Freud Museum Příbor
sources: Ernest Jones, The Life and Work of Sigmund Freud, vol. 1
Peter Gay, Freud: A Life for Our Time

stops.name: Vienna, Leopoldstadt: the family settles
stops.campa: The wool trade fails and the family drifts, first to Freiberg, then a year in Leipzig, before Jakob Freud brings his household to Vienna's Leopoldstadt, the crowded Jewish quarter across the Danube Canal. They take rooms on the Pfeffergasse, one of the poorer streets; Sigmund, not yet four, will grow up amid peddlers and pawnshops within sight of the Prater's chestnut avenues. He will call himself, all his life, a Viennese who never forgot he was first a stranger there, the immigrant's watchfulness folded permanently into the future doctor's eye.
suggested_refs: The Leopoldstadt tenements of the 1860s Jewish quarter
sources: Peter Gay, Freud: A Life for Our Time
William Johnston, The Austrian Mind

stops.name: Vienna, the Prater: the wandering poet's prophecy
stops.campa: At a restaurant garden in the Prater, where Viennese families take their Sunday air among the chestnuts, a wandering poet earns his supper improvising verses about the diners' children. He comes to the dark-haired boy Amalia calls her little Moor and, warming to the game, declares that this one will grow up to sit in the cabinet of ministers. The family repeats the story for decades, half in jest, half in earnest, the household's own small oracle, spoken over a boy who will indeed rule an empire, though not the one the poet meant.
suggested_refs: Ernest Jones's account of Freud's childhood, Life and Work vol. 1, ch. 1
sources: Ernest Jones, The Life and Work of Sigmund Freud, vol. 1
Martin Freud, Sigmund Freud: Man and Father

stops.name: Vienna: the Matura and Goethe's 'Die Natur'
stops.campa: First in his class through eight years at the Sperlgymnasium, the boy who once devoured Cervantes and taught himself Spanish for the pleasure of it now stands at the door of a profession. At a public lecture near the end of his schooling he hears Professor Carl Brühl read aloud the incomparably beautiful essay on Nature attributed to Goethe: a hymn to a Nature that creates and devours without pause or pity. The reading decides him on the spot: he will abandon the law he had half-intended and study medicine, to serve that same devouring, creating force from the inside.
stops.quote: Nature! We are surrounded and embraced by her — powerless to leave her, and powerless to enter her more deeply.
stops.quote_source: 'Die Natur' (attrib. Goethe/Tobler), recalled by Freud as decisive, An Autobiographical Study (1925)
suggested_refs: Georg Christoph Tobler's 'Die Natur' (1783), long misattributed to Goethe himself
sources: Sigmund Freud, An Autobiographical Study (1925)
Peter Gay, Freud: A Life for Our Time

stops.name: Trieste: the eel gonads
stops.campa: Sent by his zoology professor Carl Claus with a government grant, the nineteen-year-old medical student spends four weeks at the marine station of Sant'Andrea, slicing open some four hundred eels in search of the male reproductive organ that has eluded naturalists since Aristotle. He finds, in one specimen, the lobed structure he seeks hidden in the abdominal cavity, confirms what a Polish zoologist had already glimpsed, and writes his first scientific paper. It settles nothing large, but it teaches him the discipline of looking hard at what nobody else has bothered to dissect.
suggested_refs: Freud's first paper, 'Observations on the Configuration and Finer Structure of the Lobed Organs of the Eel' (1877)
sources: Historic Mysteries, 'That Time Sigmund Freud Spent Four Weeks Chopping Up Eels'
Peter Gay, Freud: A Life for Our Time

stops.name: Vienna: the medical degree
stops.campa: Three years late by his own exacting standard, distracted by physiology under Ernst Brücke, by philosophy, by a hundred tributary interests, Freud is finally awarded the degree of Doctor of Medicine by the University of Vienna. He has no taste for general practice and would rather stay in Brücke's laboratory forever measuring nerve fibers, but the physiology institute has no post to give him and poverty presses. He takes a position at the General Hospital instead, the reluctant first step from pure research toward the clinical work that will, without his yet suspecting it, remake the century's idea of the mind.
suggested_refs: Freud's MD diploma, University of Vienna, 1881
sources: Ernest Jones, The Life and Work of Sigmund Freud, vol. 1
Peter Gay, Freud: A Life for Our Time

stops.name: Paris, La Salpêtrière: Charcot's clinic
stops.campa: On a travel grant Freud crosses to Paris and spends the winter at the Salpêtrière, the great asylum-hospital where Jean-Martin Charcot, the Napoleon of the neuroses, demonstrates hysteria before crowded amphitheaters as though it were a disease of the nerves like any other, produced and abolished under hypnosis at his command. Freud watches spellbound, translates Charcot's lectures into German, and objects once, timidly, that a theory being tested does not quite fit the facts observed. Charcot's answering shrug becomes the sentence Freud will repeat for the rest of his life, against every objector to what he is about to discover.
stops.quote: Theory is good, but it doesn't prevent things from existing.
stops.quote_source: Charcot, as recalled by Freud in On the History of the Psycho-Analytic Movement (1914)
suggested_refs: Charcot's Tuesday Lessons at the Salpêtrière, later published as Leçons du mardi
sources: Sigmund Freud, An Autobiographical Study (1925)
Freud Museum London, 'Charcot'

stops.name: Vienna: the private practice opens
stops.campa: Back from Paris and burning with Charcot's example, Freud opens a private practice for nervous diseases on the Maria-Theresien-Strasse, resigning his hospital post to earn, at last, enough to marry. He advertises electrotherapy and hypnotic suggestion, the fashionable tools of the trade, though he privately suspects both will fail him; his real instrument is still being forged, in the long hours of listening to patients the Viennese medical establishment finds merely hysterical and therefore beneath serious attention. The first consulting room of psychoanalysis, before the name exists, is a rented office and a doctor's patience.
suggested_refs: Freud's first professional card, 'Dr. Sigm. Freud, Docent für Nervenkrankheiten'
sources: Peter Gay, Freud: A Life for Our Time
Ernest Jones, The Life and Work of Sigmund Freud, vol. 1

stops.name: Wandsbek, near Hamburg: the marriage to Martha Bernays
stops.campa: After a four-year engagement of poverty, jealousy, and nine hundred surviving letters, Freud marries Martha Bernays at the Wandsbek town hall, civilly, because Austrian law will not otherwise recognize the union; the religious rite follows the next day at the Wandsbek synagogue under Rabbi Hanover. Fourteen guests attend; the wedding dinner is taken at Hirschel's Hotel. They honeymoon briefly at Travemünde on the Baltic before returning to Vienna, where Martha will bear him six children in nine years and run the household that makes Berggasse 19 possible.
suggested_refs: Freud's wedding ring, engraved with Martha's name and the date 13 September 1886
sources: Freud Museum London, 'Sigmund Freud's Wedding Ring'
Peter Gay, Freud: A Life for Our Time

segments.name: Berggasse 19: the Founding of the Method

stops.name: Vienna, Berggasse 19: moving in
stops.campa: The family, Martha, the children Mathilde, Martin, and infant Oliver, moves into a newly built apartment house on the Berggasse in Vienna's ninth district, taking rooms on the mezzanine and, from 1896, an office on the floor below when space runs short. Freud will keep this address for nearly forty-seven years: the couch, the study crowded with antiquities, the consulting-room door through which two generations of patients and disciples will pass. Nothing yet marks it as sacred ground. It is simply where a struggling nerve-doctor and his young family have found an affordable, respectable flat.
suggested_refs: Berggasse 19, Vienna IX, now the Sigmund Freud Museum
sources: Sigmund Freud Museum Vienna, 'Berggasse 19'
Encyclopedia.com, 'Berggasse 19, Wien IX'

stops.name: Schloss Bellevue, near Grinzing: the secret of the dream
stops.campa: Summering at the Schloss Bellevue restaurant on the Kahlenberg slope above Grinzing, Freud dreams that his patient Irma stands before him with a throat full of white patches, and Dr. M. and two colleagues examine her while a formula for trimethylamin hovers absurdly in the air. Waking, he sees the dream not as nonsense but as a disguised wish, to be innocent of Irma's continuing illness, and begins the analysis that will anchor his whole theory of dreams. He writes to Fliess, half joking, that a marble plaque should someday mark this house as the place where the riddle of dreaming first gave up its secret.
stops.quote: In this house, on July 24th, 1895, the secret of the dream revealed itself to Dr. Sigm. Freud.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Wilhelm Fliess, 12 June 1900, imagining a future plaque
suggested_refs: The memorial plaque later erected by the Sigmund Freud Society at the site of the demolished Schloss Bellevue
sources: Letters of Sigmund Freud to Wilhelm Fliess (1887-1904)
The Interpretation of Dreams (1900), ch. 2

stops.name: Vienna: the death of Jakob Freud
stops.campa: Jakob Freud dies at eighty-one after a long decline, and his son is astonished by the depth of the grief that follows: grief mixed with something more troubling, a self-reproach he cannot at first name. In the months after the funeral Freud turns his new method of dream-analysis on his own dreams and memories, uncovering in himself the hostile wishes toward the father and the desire for the mother that he will soon name, borrowing from Sophocles, the Oedipus complex. The self-analysis undertaken at his father's grave becomes the foundation stone no other analyst's training will ever quite repeat.
stops.quote: By the time he died, his life had been over long before, but at a death the whole past stirs within one.
suggested_refs: Freud's own dream-record of his self-analysis following Jakob's death, in The Interpretation of Dreams
sources: Letters of Sigmund Freud to Wilhelm Fliess (1887-1904)
Peter Gay, Freud: A Life for Our Time

stops.name: Vienna, Berggasse 19: The Interpretation of Dreams
stops.campa: After three years of nightly self-analysis and the working-through of some two hundred of his own and his patients' dreams, Freud publishes The Interpretation of Dreams: six hundred copies, dated 1900 though it appears in November, and sold so slowly that eight years pass before a second edition is needed. In it the dream becomes the royal road to the unconscious, wish-fulfillment its grammar, condensation and displacement its syntax. Vienna's medical establishment mostly ignores it. Freud, forty-three, knows privately what he has done, and writes to Fliess that such an insight comes to a man, if it comes at all, only once in a lifetime.
stops.quote: Insight such as this falls to one's lot but once in a lifetime.
suggested_refs: The first edition of Die Traumdeutung (1899/1900), Franz Deuticke, Vienna
sources: The Interpretation of Dreams (1900)
Letters of Sigmund Freud to Wilhelm Fliess (1887-1904)

stops.name: Vienna, Berggasse 19: the Wednesday Psychological Society
stops.campa: Isolated for a decade, Freud finally gathers a circle: Wilhelm Stekel, who had been his patient, proposes it, and Freud writes short notes inviting Alfred Adler, Max Kahane, and Rudolf Reitler to his home after dinner on Wednesday evenings to discuss psychology and neuropathology over black coffee and cigars. The Wednesday Psychological Society is psychoanalysis's first congregation, meeting in the same waiting room the patients use by day. Within six years it will have fourteen members and a new name, the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society; within eleven it will have split, more than once, over the very doctrines forged at this table.
stops.quote: A small circle of colleagues and supporters afford me the great pleasure of coming to my house in the evening to discuss interesting topics in psychology and neuropathology.
suggested_refs: The minutes of the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society, later published in four volumes
sources: Freud Museum London, 'The Wednesday Psychological Society'
freudfile.org, 'The Psychoanalytical Wednesday Society'

stops.name: Lake Trasimene: the Hannibal fantasy, turning back
stops.campa: On what will be his last Italian journey for four years, Freud gets as far as Lake Trasimene, fifty miles from Rome, the very ground where Hannibal broke a Roman army in 217 BC, and turns back, unable to press on to the city he has dreamed of since boyhood. He recognizes the pattern in himself: as a schoolboy he had made Hannibal, avenger of Carthage against Rome, his favorite hero, and had sworn his own silent oath at his father's mild submission to an antisemitic insult. Now he moves into the Campagna, as Hannibal once did, and does not enter the city either.
stops.quote: I had actually been following in Hannibal's footsteps. Like him, I had been fated not to see Rome.
suggested_refs: The battlefield of Lake Trasimene, 217 BC, where Hannibal annihilated the Roman consular army
sources: The Interpretation of Dreams (1900), ch. 5
Letter to Wilhelm Fliess, 3 December 1897

stops.name: Rome: the city entered at last
stops.campa: Four years after Trasimene, at forty-five, Freud crosses into Rome with his brother Alexander and finds the phobia gone as suddenly as it came; the city yields to him with an ease that startles him more than any resistance could have. He walks the Forum, the Palatine, St. Peter's, weeks of accumulated dread dissolving into the ordinary business of sightseeing. It is, he will say afterward, among the highest experiences of his life, the resolution of a neurosis he had diagnosed in himself years before he cured it, on the same ground where he first, that day, walks as a free man among ruins.
suggested_refs: The Roman Forum and Palatine Hill, first walked by Freud on 2 September 1901
sources: Rome the Second Time, 'Freud in Rome (I) & (II)'
Peter Gay, Freud: A Life for Our Time

stops.name: Rome, San Pietro in Vincoli: the first sight of the Moses
stops.campa: In the same visit, on the Oppian Hill, Freud climbs to the church of San Pietro in Vincoli and stands for the first time before Michelangelo's seated Moses, carved for the unbuilt tomb of Pope Julius II, the prophet's head turned in fury toward the golden calf, one hand pressed into the great beard as though to stay the impulse to rise and smash the Tables of the Law. Freud says nothing of it yet in writing, but the statue enters him the way certain images do, waiting years underground before they surface as an obsession he cannot leave alone.
suggested_refs: Michelangelo's Moses, San Pietro in Vincoli, Rome, c. 1513-1515
sources: Rome the Second Time, 'Freud in Rome (II)'
Sigmund Freud, 'The Moses of Michelangelo' (1914)

segments.name: Clark University and the Crown Prince

stops.name: Vienna, Berggasse 19: the thirteen hours
stops.campa: A young Swiss asylum doctor named Carl Gustav Jung climbs the stairs of Berggasse 19 at one in the afternoon, and the two men talk almost without pause until well past midnight. Freud, fifty and already isolated by a decade of Viennese scorn, meets in this torrential younger man the first collaborator of real stature psychoanalysis has produced: a Gentile, a Protestant, a director of the Burghölzli, capable of carrying the doctrine out of the Jewish quarter of Vienna into the wider Christian world. Within the year Freud will be calling him, privately, his son and heir, the crown prince of the movement.
stops.quote: We met at one o'clock in the afternoon and talked virtually without a pause for thirteen hours.
stops.quote_source: C. G. Jung, Memories, Dreams, Reflections, ch. 5 (recalling Freud's own account of the meeting)
suggested_refs: Berggasse 19 consulting-room photographs; the Freud/Jung Letters
sources: C. G. Jung, Memories, Dreams, Reflections, ch. 5
The Freud/Jung Letters

stops.name: Vienna, Berggasse 19: the bookcase speaks
stops.campa: On Jung's second visit, in the evening study, the talk turns to precognition and the paranormal; Freud, the confirmed rationalist, answers with an impatience Jung finds too shallow. As they argue, a loud report cracks out of the nearby bookcase. Jung calls it a catalytic exteriorization of his own agitation and predicts, before Freud's astonished eyes, that it will happen again, and it does, on the instant. Freud will write it off as coincidence within weeks, unsettled less by the noise than by the vein of mysticism it exposes in the man he has anointed his successor.
stops.quote: Oh come, that is sheer bosh.
stops.quote_source: Freud's reported reply, in C. G. Jung, Memories, Dreams, Reflections, ch. 5
suggested_refs: Freud's letter to Jung on the 'poltergeist' episode, 16 April 1909
sources: C. G. Jung, Memories, Dreams, Reflections, ch. 5
The Freud/Jung Letters

stops.name: Bremen: the peat-bog dead
stops.campa: Freud, Jung, and Sándor Ferenczi meet at Bremen to board the steamer for America. At lunch Jung talks on, unable to stop, about the corpses preserved whole in the north-German peat bogs, tanned brown by the bog-water, dug up centuries later looking barely dead. Freud grows irritable, asks why Jung cares so much about corpses, and slides from his chair in a dead faint. Recovering, he tells Jung privately that he believes the talk of the dead conceals a death-wish against himself. He drinks wine that evening against his usual abstinence, uneasy, watching the younger man across the table.
suggested_refs: Moorleichen, the bog bodies of northern Europe; the SS George Washington, on which the party sailed
sources: C. G. Jung, Memories, Dreams, Reflections, ch. 5
Ernest Jones, The Life and Work of Sigmund Freud, vol. 2

stops.name: Clark University, Worcester: the New World crowned
stops.campa: At the twentieth-anniversary celebrations of Clark University, Freud delivers five lectures introducing psychoanalysis to America, sharing the platform with Jung and meeting William James, who walks apart with the younger man to speak of psychical research. On 10 September both Freud and Jung receive honorary doctorates. It is the first academic recognition psychoanalysis has ever been given anywhere, and Freud, who will later say he felt, boarding the ship home, like a duke about to enter his own dukedom, poses for the famous group photograph on the steps: the whole founding generation gathered once, and only once, together.
stops.quote: In Europe I felt as though I were despised; but over there I found myself received by the foremost men as an equal.
suggested_refs: The Clark University 1909 group photograph: Freud, Jung, James, Hall, Ferenczi, Jones
sources: Sigmund Freud, An Autobiographical Study (1925)
C. G. Jung, Memories, Dreams, Reflections, ch. 5

stops.name: Munich, Park Hotel: the faint
stops.campa: At a conference of the movement's presidents, held to patch a quarrel already opening between them, Freud and Jung talk over lunch of Amenhotep IV, who erased his own father's name from Egypt's monuments to found the worship of a single sun. Freud insists the erasure is the whole point, a parricide; Jung answers that the pharaoh was a creator, not a murderer of the father. Freud slides from his chair in a faint, the second time now, always at the same subject. Jung carries him to a couch; half-conscious, Freud murmurs of the sweetness of dying, and both men understand, without saying so, what the fainting means.
stops.quote: How sweet it must be to die.
stops.quote_source: Freud's words on waking, recorded in C. G. Jung, Memories, Dreams, Reflections, ch. 5, and Ernest Jones's Life and Work
suggested_refs: The Park Hotel, Munich; the Amenhotep IV / Akhenaten stele Freud and Jung debated
sources: Ernest Jones, The Life and Work of Sigmund Freud, vol. 2
C. G. Jung, Memories, Dreams, Reflections, ch. 5

stops.name: Munich: the last sight of each other
stops.campa: At the Fourth International Psychoanalytical Congress the movement splits visibly down the hall: Jung is re-elected president, but twenty-two delegates abstain in silent protest, and Freud and Jung pass one another in the corridors without a word. It is the last time the two men will ever see each other. Freud has already begun, in private letters, to speak of Jung's mysticism as a betrayal of the scientific discipline psychoanalysis requires; within months the correspondence that ran to hundreds of letters over six years will stop altogether, and Freud will set about writing the movement's history without its crown prince in it.
suggested_refs: The Fourth International Psychoanalytical Congress, Munich, 7-8 September 1913
sources: Ernest Jones, The Life and Work of Sigmund Freud, vol. 2
Deirdre Bair, Jung: A Biography

stops.name: Rome, San Pietro in Vincoli: three lonely weeks with Moses
stops.campa: From the wreck of Munich, Freud goes south to the church he first entered twelve years before, and for three weeks stands alone each day before Michelangelo's Moses, measuring the angle of the beard, the set of the tablets under the arm, sketching the figure until an understanding no art historian had reached dawns on him: that this is not the moment of Moses's fury at the golden calf but the moment just after, the prophet's rage already mastered and folded back into stillness by will alone. He will publish the essay anonymously, a psychoanalyst's homage disguised, fittingly, as a stranger's close reading of stone.
stops.quote: Every day for three lonely weeks of September 1913, I stood in church in front of the statue, studying it, measuring it and drawing it until there dawned on me that understanding which I expressed in my essay.
suggested_refs: Michelangelo's Moses, San Pietro in Vincoli, subject of Freud's 1914 essay
sources: Sigmund Freud, 'The Moses of Michelangelo' (1914)
Letter to Edoardo Weiss, 1933

stops.name: Vienna: 'The Moses of Michelangelo' published anonymously
stops.campa: Freud publishes the Moses essay unsigned in the third volume of Imago, the psychoanalytic journal he has founded, unwilling to attach his famous name to what he calls a mere love-child of a few weeks' leisure, a lay excursion outside medicine. The same year he sets down On the History of the Psycho-Analytic Movement, his own bitter, careful account of the schism with Adler and Jung, the founder now writing his movement's first history in order to fix, before others can distort it, exactly which departures from the doctrine count as heresy.
suggested_refs: Imago, vol. 3 (1914), where the Moses essay first appeared unsigned
sources: Sigmund Freud, 'The Moses of Michelangelo' (1914)
Sigmund Freud, On the History of the Psycho-Analytic Movement (1914)

segments.name: War, Loss, and Beyond the Pleasure Principle

stops.name: Vienna: the Great War, three sons at the front
stops.campa: War breaks out and Freud, at first swept up like most of Vienna in patriotic feeling, soon watches it with a colder eye as three of his sons, Martin, Oliver, Ernst, are called to the Austrian colors, and his practice empties of patients who can no longer afford analysis or have themselves gone to war. Coal and food run short at Berggasse 19; Freud works through the winters in an overcoat, writing the papers on metapsychology that will, once the guns fall silent, harden into a far darker theory than the one the prewar Vienna had chided him for.
suggested_refs: Freud's wartime correspondence with Lou Andreas-Salomé and Ferenczi
sources: Peter Gay, Freud: A Life for Our Time
Ernest Jones, The Life and Work of Sigmund Freud, vol. 2

stops.name: Vienna: Sophie's death
stops.campa: A telegram reaches Berggasse 19: Sophie, Freud's favorite daughter, married and living in Hamburg, has died of the influenza pneumonia still circling postwar Europe, in four or five days, in the midst of glowing health, leaving two small sons and a husband at the front too far to reach her in time. No train can carry Freud to the funeral through the coal shortages of that winter; he grieves at a distance, and writes to his friend the pastor Oskar Pfister within days, calling it a senseless, brutal stroke of fate against which there is no appeal and no consolation of faith he can honestly accept.
stops.quote: Snatched away by influenzal pneumonia, snatched away in the midst of glowing health, from a full and active life... as though she had never existed.
suggested_refs: Sophie Halberstadt-Freud (1893-1920), 'the Sunday child'
sources: Sigmund Freud, letter to Oskar Pfister, 27 January 1920
Sigmund Freud Museum, 'Freud, Spanish flu and COVID-19'

stops.name: Vienna: Beyond the Pleasure Principle
stops.campa: Written across the last war years and finished in the shadow of Sophie's death, Beyond the Pleasure Principle breaks with Freud's own earlier theory: beside the pleasure-seeking libido he now sets a death instinct, an inertia in all living matter pulling it back toward the inorganic stillness it came from. The war's compulsive, repeated nightmares of the trenches, which pleasure could never explain, are his clinical evidence; his grandson's stubborn game of throwing a reel away and reeling it back, over and over, is his domestic one. The theory scandalizes half his own circle. Freud will not retract a word of it.
stops.quote: The aim of all life is death.
suggested_refs: Freud's grandson's 'fort-da' game with a wooden reel, analyzed in the book's opening chapter
sources: Sigmund Freud, Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920)
Peter Gay, Freud: A Life for Our Time

segments.name: The Jaw and the Thirty-Three Operations

stops.name: Vienna: the first operation
stops.campa: Freud notices a leukoplakic growth on his palate and right jaw, though he has smoked twenty cigars a day for decades and will not stop even now, and has it removed by the ear-nose-throat specialist Marcus Hájek as a minor outpatient procedure, without full disclosure of what a biopsy will later confirm. The operation is botched: Freud hemorrhages twice in a wretched, understaffed recovery room, alone, unable to summon help, and later calls it the worst experience since his father's death. It is the first of what will become, over sixteen years, some thirty-three operations on the same relentless tissue.
stops.quote: Two months ago I noticed a leukoplakic growth on my jaw and palate, which I had removed.
stops.quote_source: Letter of 23 April 1923, quoted in Peter Gay, Freud: A Life for Our Time
suggested_refs: The examining table of Marcus Hájek's Vienna clinic
sources: Peter Gay, Freud: A Life for Our Time
Hektoen International, ''My dear neoplasm': Sigmund Freud's oral cancer'

stops.name: Vienna: the death of Heinele
stops.campa: Sophie's younger son, Heinz Rudolf, called Heinele, the grandson Freud has loved with an intensity he never allowed himself with his own children, dies of miliary tuberculosis after three weeks' illness, not yet five years old. Freud, who bore his father's death, the war, and his own suspected cancer without visible collapse, is undone by this one: he weeps, the only time several of his circle ever see it, and tells Ferenczi that he no longer feels much wish to go on living. He will say, years later, that he has never been the same since, and that no other death has struck him so hard.
stops.quote: For me, that child took the place of all my children and other grandchildren, and since then, since Heinele's death, I have no longer cared for my grandchildren, but find no enjoyment in life either.
suggested_refs: Heinz Rudolf 'Heinele' Halberstadt (1918-1923)
sources: Peter Gay, Freud: A Life for Our Time
Facebook / LacanCircleAustralia biographical note on Heinele

stops.name: Vienna: the radical operation and 'the Monster'
stops.campa: The biopsy confirms carcinoma. The oral surgeon Hans Pichler performs a radical two-stage operation removing most of Freud's right upper jaw and palate, leaving a cavity between mouth and nose that only an elaborate dental prosthesis can bridge. Freud calls the appliance, which he must remove and reinsert daily and which makes eating, speaking, and smoking a continual labor, simply the Monster. He learns to live inside its discomfort for the remaining sixteen years of his life, refusing morphine for the pain except at the very end, because a clouded mind, he says, is no mind for the work still in front of him.
suggested_refs: Freud's prosthesis, made by Hans Pichler and later refitted by Varaztad Kazanjian, now held at the Freud Museum London
sources: British Dental Journal, 'The prosthetic care of Sigmund Freud'
Hektoen International, ''My dear neoplasm': Sigmund Freud's oral cancer'

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main: the Goethe Prize
stops.campa: On the anniversary of Goethe's birth the city of Frankfurt awards Freud the Goethe Prize, its highest honor for German letters, recognizing the essayist and stylist as much as the doctor of the mind, the man who once decided his whole career on a schoolboy's hearing of an essay wrongly credited to the poet. Too ill to travel, Freud sends Anna to Frankfurt to receive it in his place; the mayor praises a genius that has carried German science to the far corners of the earth. Freud calls it privately the high point of his public life, an official blessing from the culture that will, within a decade, burn his books.
suggested_refs: The Goethe Prize medal, Frankfurt am Main, awarded annually since 1927
sources: Jewish Telegraphic Agency, 'Sigmund Freud Awarded 1930 Goethe Prize'
Peter Gay, Freud: A Life for Our Time

stops.name: Vienna, Berggasse 19: the Anschluss
stops.campa: Three days after German troops cross into Austria to a delirious welcome, an armed platoon searches Berggasse 19, rifling through the apartment and the publishing house Freud has built for his works, taking a sum of money from Martha's household cashbox on their way out. Freud, eighty-one, refuses at first to believe the danger is total; friends and disciples abroad, Ernest Jones foremost, begin at once, over his objections, to arrange an exit he does not yet want. Within a week the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society itself will be dissolved by government order, its forty-year archive in immediate peril.
suggested_refs: The Sigmund Freud Museum's exhibit 'Raids in Berggasse'
sources: Sigmund Freud Museum, 'Raids in Berggasse'
Library of Congress, 'Freud's Last Days in Vienna as Nazis Approached'

stops.name: Vienna: Anna's arrest
stops.campa: The Gestapo returns and this time takes Anna Freud to their headquarters at the former Hotel Metropol on the Morzinplatz for questioning about the international psychoanalytic association's finances. She and her brother Martin have already obtained a lethal dose of Veronal from the family doctor Max Schur, in case interrogation turns to torture or internment. Anna returns unharmed that evening after hours under the lamp, but her father's diary entry that day, four laconic words, records the moment his resistance to leaving finally breaks, once and for all, for good.
stops.quote: Anna bei Gestapo. [Anna at the Gestapo.]
suggested_refs: Freud's terse diary, kept 1929-1939, now in the Library of Congress
sources: The Diary Review, 'Anna with Gestapo'
amNY, 'Twelve hours of Anna Freud under a Nazi interrogation lamp'

stops.name: Vienna: the Orient Express, 3:25 in the afternoon
stops.campa: After nearly three months of exit visas, a punitive 'flight tax,' and William Bullitt's diplomatic pressure on the Reich through the American consulate, Freud, Martha, and Anna board the Orient Express out of Vienna. Freud's own note records only the bare fact: departure, 3:25. He sends word to Arnold Zweig that opens with two words. Behind him stay four elderly sisters who will not obtain exit papers in time and will die, within a few years, in the camps at Theresienstadt, Treblinka, and Auschwitz: a debt his own escape carries and can never discharge.
stops.quote: Leaving today for 39 Elsworthy Road, London N.W.3.
suggested_refs: Freud's 1938 travel diary, recording the departure and the Rhine crossing at Kehl
sources: Freud Museum London, 'Leaving Today: the Freuds in Exile 1938'
Andrew Nagorski, 'The Rescue of Sigmund Freud'

stops.name: Paris: the stopover with Marie Bonaparte
stops.campa: The train crosses the German frontier at Kehl and runs on through France; in Paris the family breaks the journey at the house of Princess Marie Bonaparte, Freud's analysand and devoted friend, who has already done much of the quiet, expensive work that made the exit possible at all: ransom, guarantees, and favors called in with French and British officials. She will do the same, within the year, for Freud's sisters, too late for most of them. At her table Freud rests for a day among his own antiquities, already partly crated and shipped ahead, before the last short leg across the Channel.
suggested_refs: Marie Bonaparte's house on the rue Adolphe-Yvon, Paris
sources: Freud Museum London, 'Leaving Today: the Freuds in Exile 1938'
Peter Gay, Freud: A Life for Our Time

stops.name: London: landfall in exile
stops.campa: Freud reaches London on 6 June, met at Victoria Station by a small, relieved crowd of English colleagues, and takes temporary rooms at 39 Elsworthy Road in Hampstead while a permanent house is found. He is eighty-two, in constant pain from the cancer, and has lost his home of forty-seven years, his language of daily life, and most of his sisters' safety in a single season, yet he writes almost at once that the relief of feeling, for the first time since March, that no knock at the door can mean the Gestapo, outweighs everything else that has been lost.
stops.quote: The feeling of triumph on being liberated is too strongly mixed with grief.
suggested_refs: Freud's arrival at Victoria Station, London, photographed 6 June 1938
sources: Freud Museum London, 'Leaving Today: the Freuds in Exile 1938'
Peter Gay, Freud: A Life for Our Time

stops.name: London, 20 Maresfield Gardens: the couch reassembled
stops.campa: The family moves into a tall red-brick house in Hampstead, 20 Maresfield Gardens, and Freud's study is rebuilt almost exactly as Berggasse 19 had stood: the same crowded shelves of Egyptian, Greek, and Roman antiquities, the same rug-covered analytic couch, the same desk facing the garden. He resumes seeing a handful of patients within weeks of arrival, working now against the clock of his illness on Moses and Monotheism, the strange last book in which the founder of psychoanalysis argues that Moses himself was an Egyptian, and that monotheism's God is the murdered father returning, endlessly, in the guilt of the sons.
suggested_refs: 20 Maresfield Gardens, now the Freud Museum London; Freud's study, reconstructed with the original antiquities and couch
sources: Freud Museum London
Sigmund Freud, Moses and Monotheism (1939)

stops.name: London, Maresfield Gardens: the end
stops.campa: By September the cancer, declared inoperable months before, has eaten through the cheek into a wound that will not heal, the pain no longer bearable and no longer, Freud says, making any sense. He tells his physician Max Schur he wishes to be released, asks him to consult Anna, and Schur, keeping a promise made years earlier never to let him suffer needlessly, administers morphine on the night of the 21st and again on the 22nd. Freud dies in the small hours of 23 September 1939, eleven days after Hitler's armies cross into Poland, the century he diagnosed already at war around him.
stops.quote: Now it is nothing but torture and makes no sense any more.
stops.quote_source: Freud to Max Schur, September 1939, recounted in Schur, Freud: Living and Dying (1972)
suggested_refs: Freud's ashes, in a Greek krater given by Marie Bonaparte, at Golders Green Crematorium
sources: Max Schur, Freud: Living and Dying (1972)
Freud Museum London, 'Freud's Death Bed'
